questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What an authority is asserting
questions.learningObjective: Describe what a certification document asserts about the design it covers
questions.stem: An architect's brief describes a review where an outside body issues a document stating that a design satisfies the published rules. What is that document asserting?

options.text: That the design has been checked against a named set of rules by someone with authority to judge them
That the design is safe in every possible future and can never need changes
options.misconception: reads an approval as a guarantee of future performance

options.text: That the designer no longer carries any responsibility for the design that was approved
options.misconception: believes approval transfers all liability away

options.text: That the design will be built exactly as drawn, since approval guarantees the workmanship
options.misconception: confuses document approval with construction quality

questions.explanation: A certification document records that a body with authority examined this design against the stated rules and found it conforming. The tempting options read it as a lifetime guarantee, a discharge of duty or a promise about workmanship.
questions.hint: Ask what was examined and by whom.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Where trust has to be given deliberately
questions.learningObjective: Identify the entry that makes the trust decision explicit
questions.stem: An architect's brief lists the bodies a building system is allowed to trust. Which entry makes the trust decision explicit?

options.text: A note that any certificate should be accepted if it is well formed
options.misconception: treats a well formed certificate as trustworthy

options.text: A named entry for each body whose certificates the system will accept, kept in a controlled list
A note that the body which issued the certificate must be contacted before each use
options.misconception: requires contacting issuers instead of listing them

options.text: A note that trust is granted to whichever body issues the next certificate
options.misconception: grants trust automatically to the newest issuer

questions.explanation: Trust becomes a deliberate decision when the acceptable bodies are named in a list the team controls and reviews. The tempting options accept anything well formed, rely on contacting issuers or hand trust to whoever speaks next.
questions.hint: Ask where the acceptable bodies are named.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a name check establishes
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a host name check establishes and what it misses
questions.stem: An architect's brief asks the building system to check that a certificate names the host it is talking to. Explain what such a name check establishes and what it does not.

answer.exemplar: Matching the name in the certificate against the host being contacted shows that the certificate was issued for this machine and not for some other one, which stops a valid certificate from another host being replayed here. It says nothing about whether the certificate came from a trustworthy issuer, which is a separate question about the chain of trust.

questions.explanation: The name check binds the certificate to the host in front of the client, which is a question about addressing rather than about the issuer. The tempting wrong idea is that a matching name also proves the issuer is trustworthy.
questions.hint: Ask which question the name answers and which it leaves open.

questions.hint: Subtract the elapsed days from the window.

questions.topic: A certificate for a different host

questions.stem: Given the brief, what happens when the lift controller receives a certificate that names a sibling controller instead of its own host?

options.text: The certificate must be accepted, because it comes from the same trusted issuer
options.misconception: treats a shared issuer as sufficient for acceptance

options.text: The certificate must be accepted, because both controllers sit in the same basement
options.misconception: accepts proximity as a substitute for a name match

options.text: The certificate must be rejected, because it does not name the host the controller is
The certificate must be accepted, because the supplier issues all of them
options.misconception: accepts a shared supplier as a substitute for a name match

questions.explanation: A certificate issued for a different host is refused, because the brief makes the name the deciding test. The tempting options accept it on the strength of the issuer, the location or the supplier instead.

options.text: The chain reaches a body whose certificate on the site was issued most recently
options.misconception: mistakes recency for trustworthiness

options.misconception: reads the subject field as a trust decision

options.text: The chain reaches a body that the client has explicitly listed as trusted

questions.explanation: A chain is only useful to the client if it ends at a body the client chose to trust, and that is the point the walk is looking for. The tempting options treat rarity, recency or a field inside the certificate as the trust decision.

options.misconception: accepts an expired certificate as usable

options.misconception: treats any root as a trusted one

questions.explanation: A name that belongs to another host is refused even when the issuer is trusted, which shows the two checks are distinct. The tempting options let one check stand in for another or accept a failure outright.

options.misconception: invents an external certificate the design does not use

options.misconception: credits the name check with the issuer check's job

options.text: It shows the certificate is still inside its valid period
options.misconception: credits the name check with the validity check's job

It shows the private key is held by the device that presented it

options.misconception: treats a future start date as a trust failure

options.text: A certificate whose valid period ended last year, issued by a body the site does not trust
options.misconception: refuses on two grounds instead of the valid period alone

questions.learningObjective: State the principle behind an explicit list of trusted bodies
questions.stem: An architect's brief says the building system keeps a list of the bodies whose certificates it will accept and never accepts a certificate otherwise. Which principle does that implement?

options.text: Trust is granted to any body that can show a complete chain to some root
options.misconception: grants trust on chain completeness alone

options.text: Trust is granted to the body that issued the most recent certificate on the site
options.misconception: confuses recency with trustworthiness

options.text: Trust is granted automatically to every body that appears in a certificate chain
options.misconception: spreads trust along chains without a decision

options.text: Trust is granted explicitly to named bodies and is not extended automatically to anyone else

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A certificate past its valid period
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an expired certificate is refused by default
questions.stem: Under the architect's guidance the client refuses a controller certificate whose valid period has ended. Explain what an expired certificate tells the client and why refusing it is the right default.

answer.exemplar: An expired certificate may have been issued when the key was safe, so it no longer shows that the holder today is entitled to be trusted, and it is a known, dated weakness that an attacker can count on. Refusing it by default keeps the client from depending on a guarantee the issuer has already withdrawn, even where the key itself was never compromised.

questions.explanation: The date tells the client that the issuer no longer stands behind the certificate, which is a reason to refuse it even if the key was sound. The tempting wrong idea is that an unexpired key is all that matters.
questions.hint: Ask what the date adds to the key's standing.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A certificate for a different host
questions.learningObjective: Explain the risk of skipping the host name comparison
questions.stem: The host comparison in the brief matches the name in the certificate with the host being contacted. Explain what goes wrong if the client skips that comparison.

answer.exemplar: Without the name comparison, a certificate that is validly signed and issued by a trusted body for some other device on the same estate would still be accepted here, so an attacker with one legitimate device could present it and be taken for another. The chain check would pass because the issuer really is trusted, which is exactly why the separate name check exists.

questions.explanation: The chain check confirms the issuer, not the target, so without the name comparison a valid certificate for another device passes everywhere. The tempting wrong idea is that a trusted issuer makes the target irrelevant.
questions.hint: Ask what the chain check does not tell you.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Where trust has to be given deliberately
questions.learningObjective: Explain why giving trust deliberately matters in a building
questions.stem: For the building's security design the client is configured with a named list and the brief warns that adding an entry has consequences. Explain why giving trust deliberately matters in a building.

answer.exemplar: Trust is a decision about which bodies may speak for the building's systems, and every entry extends what an attacker can obtain if that body's key is ever compromised. Keeping the list explicit makes the exposure visible and reviewable, rather than letting trust spread silently along whatever chain a certificate happens to present.

questions.explanation: Every trusted body widens the surface a compromise could reach, so the set has to be a visible decision with an owner. The tempting wrong idea treats an inherited or automatic trust as harmless.
questions.hint: Ask what grows every time a body is added.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the limits of pinning on a controlled fleet
questions.stem: In the closed building system the brief has controllers sign their own certificates and the client is told in advance which to accept. Explain why this can be sound on a controlled fleet and what limits it.

answer.exemplar: On a fleet the operator controls, the client can pin each device's own certificate in advance, so no external issuer is needed and the chain stops at the device itself. questions.explanation: Pinning is sound because the operator controls both ends and decides every accepted certificate in advance. The tempting wrong idea is that the scheme scales or survives replacement without any upkeep.

questions.explanation: Only a body named in the client's list is trusted; past use, appearance in a chain or volume of stored certificates carry no standing. The tempting options each substitute a signal for the decision itself.
questions.hint: Ask what the list actually names.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a name check establishes
questions.learningObjective: Compute the storage used by accepted host names
questions.stem: An architect's brief says each controller hosts a list of 25 accepted names, and each entry on that list holds a name of 40 characters. How many characters are stored across the whole list?
questions.explanation: Twenty-five names of 40 characters each take 1000 characters. The tempting answer counts the names alone and gives 25, ignoring the length of each entry.
questions.hint: Multiply the entries by the characters in each.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A certificate past its valid period
questions.learningObjective: Identify a certificate that should be refused because its date has passed

stimulus.body: An architect's brief says certificates are valid for one year and the client's list of trusted bodies is reviewed every six months. The brief records that one controller kept presenting a certificate that had been valid for two years.

questions.stem: Given the brief, what does the behaviour of that controller tell you?

options.text: The controller is presenting a certificate that the client must accept because its issuer is trusted
options.misconception: lets issuer trust override the expiry

options.text: The controller is showing that the client's trust list has been changed without notice
options.misconception: invents a trust list change the brief does not mention

options.text: The controller is presenting a certificate that was renewed automatically at the halfway point
options.misconception: invents an automatic renewal the brief does not mention

options.text: The controller is presenting a certificate the client should refuse because its valid period has ended

questions.explanation: A certificate presented two years after a one-year validity has ended, so the client refuses it whatever the issuer's standing. The tempting options override the expiry or invent renewals and list changes.
questions.hint: Ask how long the brief says a certificate lasts.
